worksheet.title: Find and Fix
worksheet.subtitle: Different programs, different bugs
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find what kind of bug a program has and fix it.

parts.title: Bugs come in different kinds
parts.text: A bug can be a wrong block, an extra block, a missing block, or the wrong order. Read each program, run it, figure out the kind of bug, and fix it so Bit reaches the target.

parts.title: Find and fix A
parts.prompt: Run Program A from 1. Where does Bit land? It misses 4. Fix the program so Bit reaches 4 — what did you change?

parts.title: Find and fix B
parts.prompt: Run Program B from 0. Where does Bit land? It misses 3. Fix the program so Bit reaches 3 — what did you change?

parts.title: You try — name the bug
parts.prompt: Each program had a different kind of bug. What kind of bug was in Program A? What kind was in Program B?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A good debugger figures out WHAT kind of bug it is — wrong, extra, missing, or out of order — and then fixes that kind. Run the code again to make sure.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students diagnose and fix two programs with DIFFERENT kinds of bugs — a wrong block and an extra block — then name each bug type. Telling apart the kind of bug is a big step in debugging. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: tape a number line 0 to 5 on the floor and mark the target, so students can walk the buggy program and feel Bit miss.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Remind them of the bug types: a wrong block, an extra block, a missing block, a wrong-way block.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Program A misses 4; the fix is to change a block's number.
3. Let them try. Students fix Program B (Ex 2), then name each bug type (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Program A: 1, forward 1 → 2 (misses 4). Bug = wrong block; change forward 1 to forward 3 so 1 → 4.
Exercise 2 — Program B: 0 → 2 → 3 → 4 (misses 3). Bug = an extra block; remove one forward 1 so 0 → 2 → 3.
Exercise 3 — Program A had a wrong block (wrong number); Program B had an extra block.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: applying the same fix to both. Each program has a different kind of bug.
Make it easier: ask first "did Bit fall short, go too far, or go the wrong way?"
Make it harder: ask them to write a third program with a missing-block bug.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students follow (or write) step-by-step instructions, in order, to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a program, change a block to fix it, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child fixes both programs and names the wrong-block and extra-block bug types.
